# # Simulating Deletions

import pandas
from time import time

from cobra.io import load_model
from cobra.flux_analysis import (
    single_gene_deletion, single_reaction_deletion, double_gene_deletion,
    double_reaction_deletion)

cobra_model = load_model("textbook")
ecoli_model = load_model("iJO1366")

# ## Knocking out single genes and reactions

# A commonly asked question when analyzing metabolic models is what will happen if a certain reaction was not allowed to have any flux at all. This can tested using cobrapy by

print('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())
with cobra_model:
    cobra_model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()
    print('pfk knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())

# For evaluating genetic manipulation strategies, it is more interesting to examine what happens if given genes are knocked out as doing so can affect no reactions in case of redundancy, or more reactions if gene when is participating in more than one reaction.

print('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())
with cobra_model:
    cobra_model.genes.b1723.knock_out()
    print('pfkA knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())
    cobra_model.genes.b3916.knock_out()
    print('pfkB knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())

# ## Single Deletions

# Perform all single gene deletions on a model

deletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)

# These can also be done for only a subset of genes

single_gene_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[:20])

# This can also be done for reactions

single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[:20])

# ## Double Deletions

# Double deletions run in a similar way.

double_gene_deletion(
    cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[-5:]).round(4)

# By default, the double deletion function will automatically use multiprocessing, splitting the task over up to 4 cores if they are available. The number of cores can be manually specified as well. Setting use of a single core will disable use of the multiprocessing library, which often aids debugging.

start = time()  # start timer()
double_gene_deletion(
    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=2)
t1 = time() - start
print("Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in "
      "%.2f sec with 2 cores" % t1)

start = time()  # start timer()
double_gene_deletion(
    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=1)
t2 = time() - start
print("Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in "
      "%.2f sec with 1 core" % t2)

print("Speedup of %.2fx" % (t2 / t1))

# Double deletions can also be run for reactions.

double_reaction_deletion(
    cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[2:7]).round(4)

# ## Accessing individual deletion results
#
# Note that the indices for deletions are python [set](https://docs.python.org/3.8/library/stdtypes.html#set-types-set-frozenset) objects. This is the appropriate type since the order of deletions does not matter. Deleting reaction 1 and reaction 2 will have the same effect as deleting reaction 2 and reaction 1. 
#
# To make it easier to access results all DataFrames returned by COBRAPpy deletion functions have a `knockout` indexer that makes that a bit simpler. Each entry in the indexer is treated as a single deletion entry. So you need to pass sets for double deletions.

single = single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)
double = double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)

print(single.knockout["ATPM"])
print(double.knockout[{"ATPM", "TKT1"}])

# This can be used to get several deletions at once and will also work for Reaction or Gene objects (depending on what you deleted) directly.

atpm = cobra_model.reactions.ATPM
tkt1 = cobra_model.reactions.TKT1
pfk = cobra_model.reactions.PFK

print(single.knockout[atpm, tkt1, pfk])
print(double.knockout[{atpm, tkt1}, {atpm, pfk}, {atpm}])

specification.review:
# Private review

## Scope and endpoint selection
The notebook's terminal scientific products are systematic in-silico FBA deletion analyses of the complete E. coli core ("textbook") model, plus the interpreted single-knockout demonstrations in the first section. Selected endpoints (all on the unmodified textbook model, default FBA method):

1. `single_gene_deletions.csv` ← `deletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-50).
2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv` ← `single = single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-96).
3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv` ← `double = double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-97).
4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv` ← the printed context-block optima (calls 32–44): wild-type, PFK reaction knockout, b1723 knockout, b1723+b3916 simultaneous knockout. The plan.json marked these endpoint-unavailable for append-only export; per the endpoint-recovery policy these are recovered as an assigned task output computed from the same supplied model by the same methods (the with-blocks restore the model, so no hidden state is involved). PFK- and b1723-row values are projections of tables 2 and 1 respectively; the wild-type optimum and the b1723+b3916 double-gene combination are not subsumed by any export, so they must be kept.

## Source-operation coverage ledger
- call-25 `load_model("textbook")` — model supplied as task input (see handoff).
- calls 26, 69, 70, 72–80, 76, 77 (`iJO1366` runs, `time()`, speedup print) — excluded as nondeterministic multiprocessing timing benchmark; narrative frames them solely as such ("Speedup of %.2fx"). Note the print text "200 genes" contradicts the 25-gene slice; text bug in the notebook, diagnostic either way.
- calls 54 (`genes[:20]`), 58 (`reactions[:20]`) — subtree demonstrations; subsumed by projections of tables 1/2 (same populations restricted to prefixes; narrative: "These can also be done for only a subset").
- calls 64–65 (`double_gene_deletion(genes[-5:]).round(4)`) — mechanics demonstration of the double-deletion API on a positional 5-gene slice, value discarded (not stored, and not even printed in the script run — bare expression, absent from the reference log), `.round(4)` is display formatting. Excluded as teaching mechanics; the narrative does not interpret its results. Residual judgment call noted for validation; recovery by faithful recomputation would be possible if reviewers disagree.
- calls 87–88 (`reactions[2:7]`) — subsumed by projection of table 3.
- calls 99–100, 108–109 (`.knockout` indexer prints) — reads of rows of tables 2/3; subsumed by stated projections.
- calls 32–44 — recovered as table 4 above.

## Method facts verified in pinned code (cobra/0.32.1 wheels)
- `deletion.py` line 208: population `= {frozenset(comb) for comb in product(*element_lists)}`; both entity lists default to the full model reaction/gene list, so the double-reaction population contains each set {r_i, r_j} over all ordered pairs (r, r) → singletons included). Observed: 95 + C(95,2) = 4560 rows; single tables 137 and 95 rows (structural audit; private cross-check).
- Row construction `(set(ids), growth, status)`, growth from `slim_optimize()` under default `method="fba"`; `SolverError` → NaN growth + solver status (observed statuses in audit: "optimal", "infeasible" only).
- `Gene.knock_out` (core/gene.py 240–251): Functional→False, zeroes bounds of associated reactions left non-functional per GPR. `Reaction.knock_out`: bounds (0,0), both directions.
- `args` is a set of frozensets ⇒ row emission order is set-iteration order, run-dependent. Scientific invariance: order is meaningless.

## Observed fidelity / replay
Reference execution (exit 0, ~12 s, GPUless, offline-capable — models bundle in cobra package data per outcome.json) produced the three CSVs with columns knockouts/growth/status, hashed in trial/result.json and output-audit.json. Replay runs show identical headers and stable row counts but differing byte hashes and differing row-multiset fingerprints — explained by run-dependent row order (set iteration) and low-order float digit variation between solves (multiple alternating optima / LP degeneracy; e.g. 0.9166474637510491 vs ...509). Tiny negative growth values present (single tables min ≈ -3.7e-15, double ≈ -6.8e-14) and retained unrounded in the reference — no clamping. These are serialization/noise observations, not a calibrated comparison contract; tolerance calibration belongs to validation.

## Blockers / defects
- Table 4 (`pfk_knockout_optima.csv`) has no existing reference artifact; construction must generate it by faithful recomputation of the original with-block calls on the same model and it needs independent validation. Reference stdout (private) records 0.874 / 0.704 / 0.874 / 0.704 printed optima, cross-consistent with tables 1–2 projections, but stdout is not a ground-truth substitute.
- Task input (textbook SBML) is not yet materialized; see validation handoff. Draft is contingent on that materialization and on grading validation.

No other unresolved scientific definitional gaps. Exclusions and subsumptions are source-backed as cited above.
specification.task_brief:
# Growth effects of gene and reaction knockouts in the E. coli core metabolic model

## Objective

You are given the curated "textbook" E. coli core metabolic model (SBML). Using flux balance analysis (FBA), determine how every possible single-gene deletion, single-reaction deletion and pairwise reaction deletion affects the maximal achievable growth (the maximum of the model's biomass objective), plus the growth of a few specific knockouts that illustrate gene-level redundancy (isozymes) for phosphofructokinase.

For each knockout scenario the quantity of interest is the optimal value of the model's biomass objective after the knockout is applied, together with the status reported by the LP solve ("optimal" or "infeasible").

## Supplied inputs

- `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` — the E. coli core metabolic model in SBML format (the model known as "textbook" / BiGG `e_coli_core`), including its biomass objective reaction and gene–protein–reaction (GPR) associations. Use the model exactly as supplied; do not modify it, its medium, bounds or objective.

## Knockout semantics

- **Reaction knockout**: the reaction is deleted from any flux-carrying solution — its flux is constrained to zero in both directions.
- **Gene knockout**: a reaction is disabled only if its GPR rule evaluates to false with the knocked-out gene(s) removed. If a reaction has an isozyme gene that remains functional (e.g. an OR in the GPR), the reaction still carries flux. A gene whose removal disables no reaction therefore has no growth effect even though the gene is knocked out.

## Required outputs

Produce four CSV files. All use the columns `knockouts,growth,status`:

- `knockouts`: the identifier(s) of the knocked-out entity (gene id or reaction id, exactly as defined in the supplied model), sorted lexicographically and joined with `;` (e.g. `b1723;b3916`, `Biomass_Ecoli_core;LDH_D`). For a knockout of a single entity the label is just that entity's id.
- `growth`: the optimal objective value of the LP after the knockout, as reported by the solver at full double precision, with no rounding, clamping or sign correction (tiny negative numerical values of magnitude ~1e-14 that arise from solver noise are expected and must be reported as-is). If the knockout makes the problem infeasible, leave this field empty.
- `status`: the LP solve status string, e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`.

### 1. `single_gene_deletions.csv`
One row for **every gene defined in the supplied model** (including genes whose deletion disables no reaction), reporting the effect of knocking out that gene alone.

### 2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv`
One row for **every reaction defined in the supplied model** (this includes boundary/exchange reactions), reporting the effect of knocking out that reaction alone.

### 3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv`
One row for **each distinct set of one or two reactions** obtained by pairing every reaction in the model with every reaction in the model and reducing the pair to an unordered set. Concretely: for all ordered pairs (r_i, r_j) over the model's full reaction list, the resulting knockout sets {r_i, r_j}; the i = j cases contribute the single-reaction sets {r_i}. Do not apply gene-level GPR logic here — both reactions are knocked out directly. Report growth and status for each set.

### 4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv`
Four rows, using the same column convention, with an empty `knockouts` field for the no-knockout row:

| knockouts | scenario |
|---|---|
| *(empty)* | wild-type model, no knockout |
| `PFK` | the PFK reaction knocked out |
| `b1723` | gene b1723 (pfkA) knocked out |
| `b1723;b3916` | genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously |

These quantify the redundancy narrative: the isozyme pfkB can compensate for a pfkA deletion, but not when both are removed.

## Conventions

- Row order in every file carries no scientific meaning; any row ordering is acceptable.
- Growth is reported in the model's native biomass-objective units (the raw LP objective value).
- Use the knockout populations exactly as defined above; do not skip entities that have no reaction associations or no growth effect.
- Do not round any value (`growth` is written at full double precision).

## Environment and resources

- CPU only (up to 4 cores), 8 GiB RAM, 10 GiB disk, no network access. Your program must complete within 600 seconds.
- A reference Python environment (cobrapy 0.32.1 with the GLPK solver) can be supplied for convenience, but any software stack that satisfies the definitions above is acceptable; the results, not the tool, are what is compared.
- Exact acceptance criteria (including numerical tolerances appropriate for LP-solver variation) are finalized separately during validation before the contract takes effect; produce results faithful to the definitions above.
